NYC Office Conversions Charge Ahead After Summer Scare
 
Plus, the little-known real-estate business riding high on AI
 
By Craig Karmin
 

This is an edition of the Real Estate newsletter, a weekly briefing of the biggest commercial deals, news, analysis and trends in office, multifamily, retail and other commercial sectors. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

In July, a major New York City office-to-residential conversion project risked partial collapse after two support pillars buckled. The city evacuated surrounding buildings and the conversion process at the former Pfizer headquarters was halted. Today, the city is revving up its conversion engine once again. The Department of Buildings concluded that the accident was specific to that one property and didn’t reflect an inherent risk related to conversions. Since the accident, the department has issued initial construction permits for 16 new projects, Peter Grant reports. Even with rising interest rates making these projects more difficult to pencil out, New York needs housing. Read why conversions remain a popular vehicle.

 

One of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom is a barely known commercial real-estate business. Industrial outdoor storage provides yards for stowing construction equipment, materials, and delivery vehicles. Owners of these facilities are getting more business than they can handle because the U.S. has a scarcity of properties to accommodate the recent explosion in data centers. Rent prices are up more than 110% since 2020 across the top eight markets. Will Parker explains who the biggest winners are in the investment community.

 
 
 

NYC’s Office-Conversion Projects Are Back After a Big Summer Scare

 
 
ANGELINA KATSANIS/ASSOCIATED PRESS
 

New York City’s conversion boom is revving up again, only months after a near-disaster in Midtown Manhattan halted work on a major project and sparked new safety questions about turning office towers into housing.

 
 
 

The Once-Obscure Corner of Commercial Real Estate Now Riding the AI Boom

 
 
STEEL PEAK
 

One of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom is a barely known commercial real-estate business. 

 

Demand for industrial outdoor storage—or yards used for stowing construction equipment, materials, and delivery vehicles—is soaring alongside the rapid build-out of data centers.

 
 
 
100,000
 

The number of truckloads of steel, concrete, generators and equipment required for every gigawatt of data center capacity built, according to DAT Freight and Analytics.

 
 
 

Data Points

 

• 2,352: The number of extended stay projects in some stage of development, accounting for about 40% of the overall U.S. hotel construction pipeline, according to Lodging Econometrics. This hotel category has been growing recently as operators target longer-term guests.

 

• 276.8 million: The square footage of industrial space leased in the third quarter, a 27% increase compared with a year ago, according to CBRE. Manufacturing and data center-related firms are driving demand for industrial and logistics space.

 

• 5.9%: Minneapolis apartment vacancy at the end of the third quarter, according to CoStar. That is well below the city’s 8% peak vacancy rate in 2024 after an apartment construction wave in the city.
